description: One-person team for Daniel Gu, a 5th grade student from Rocketry Creations, building a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge in Irvine, CA (Virtual).
summary: On the Moon or Mars, astronauts must grow their own fresh food — but in space there is no gravity to pull water down to a plant's roots, so watering is a real problem. I designed and built the Space Plant Irrigation System to solve it, and to train junior astronauts to care for plants the way real crews will. At its heart is a control board I designed and soldered myself, built around an ESP32. A soil-moisture sensor checks the soil; when it gets dry, the controller turns on a pump and waters the plant automatically, then stops at the right level. My PlantHub dashboard shows live moisture, pump, grow-light, and fan status, and every reading is logged. The plant chamber provides light and moving air, and the system runs on solar power. It works by itself — and it teaches students, hands-on, how food will be grown beyond Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works: The Space Plant Irrigation System keeps a plant alive automatically, the way a crew on the Moon or Mars would need it to. A soil-moisture sensor buried in the soil reports how wet the soil is to a control board I designed and soldered myself, built around an ESP32. When the moisture drops below 40%, the controller switches on a small pump, which pushes water from a reservoir through a tube to the plant's roots. When the soil reaches 45%, the pump stops — never too much, never too little. A real-time clock and SD card log every reading, so the whole history of the plant can be reviewed. My PlantHub web dashboard shows live soil moisture, pump, grow-light and ventilation-fan status, and lets me control each one manually when I want to. The plant grows in a chamber with LED grow lights and a fan for moving air, and the system is powered by a solar panel.

Benefits: The system waters by itself, day and night, using measured amounts of water — important in space, where every drop is recycled and astronaut time is precious. The logged data turns plant care into real mission data that students can read and learn from.

Intended impact: This project is a hands-on trainer for junior astronauts. Growing fresh food will be essential on long missions — for nutrition and for morale — and students who train with this system learn the actual skills involved: sensing, automation, and caring for living things in a closed environment.

Tools, hardware, and software: ESP32 microcontroller on my own custom control board (designed in EasyEDA, soldered by hand), soil-moisture sensor, water pump and tubing, RTC clock module, microSD card logging, LED grow lights, ventilation fan, solar panel, and a web dashboard I built to monitor and control it all. The controller code is my own.

Creativity: Instead of a watering gadget, I built a miniature space habitat for one plant — with its own control board, mission-style dashboard, and data log, like a tiny version of what real space agencies are testing.

Factors I considered: In space, there is no gravity, so water must be delivered carefully at the roots in exact amounts; water and power are limited, so the system had to be efficient and solar-powered; plants need light and moving air, not just water; and the system had to be reliable enough to keep the plant alive even when nobody is watching it.

That covers every question in the prompt — how it works, benefits, impact, tools, creativity, and the factors (no gravity, limited water and power, plant needs, reliability).
